newsitem.title: UK: Markets unfazed by stability pact saga -- so far.
newsitem.headline: Markets unfazed by stability pact saga -- so far.

text.p: A dispute among European leaders over how to keep public finances in order has done little to dim optimism in the markets over prospects for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
German calls for a strict fining system within a so-called stability pact have met with opposition from other potential members of a single currency, including EMU powerhouse France.
But economists on Tuesday said unless the dispute erupts into a full-fledged row, markets will continue to bet on yields converging in Europe. The main potential loser? The mark.

"There clearly will be a compromise," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam. "With the number of sides involved with the dispute there has to be a compromise."
Thurday's meeting of European Union finance ministers will offer a last chance to iron out differences between Germany and others before an EU summit in Dublin on Friday and Saturday.

Economists said Germany appears practically isolated and will have to accept a scaled down version of the punishing system it originally wanted. The stability pact is designed to ensure EMU members maintain fiscal discipline after the start of a single currency, slated for 1999.

"Convergence (of European long-term interest rates) theoretically should be at risk, but any agreement means EMU is more likely to go ahead, which is positive for convergence," Venables said. The bigger threat lay in the foreign exchanges.
"The degree of dilution for the German plan could have definite undertones for the mark," he said.

Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase in London, said markets will probably be satisfied as long as they get something out of the Dublin summit, whether it be a defined stability pact or promising noises about reaching agreement on one. "In terms of convergence, as long as EMU is going ahead on time, they will be happy to continue to buy Spain and Italy and Portugal," he said.
The dramatic convergence of long-term rates in these typically high-yielding countries towards Bunds has been the dominant feature in bond markets throughout 1996.
The spread between Italian and German 10-year yields, for instance, has narrowed to around 1.75 percentage points on Tuesday from 4.75 points at the start of the year.

"The only problem is if it (the pact) is watered down too much it may raise doubts about whether the German constitutional court will see the stability pact as being rigorous enough," Gunner said. "They (the German court) can still torpedo the whole thing."

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said after a one-day summit with France on Monday that the two countries planned to reveal a joint position on the budget pact in the next few days. But he gave no indication the sides had moved closer together.
France is seen to be fighting for some leeway on the terms at which the target can be exceeded for the three percent deficit-to-GDP ratio, as laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.

"As long as there are some numbers there, like the three percent deficit, and there is some kind of facility to penalise countries -- even though it may not be as automatic as Germany wants -- it will be enough to keep things on track and the markets will be happy with that," Chase's Gunner said.
While few expect the stability pact wranglings to deteriorate into an unseemly fight, economists say there is still plenty at stake for markets.

"An awful lot of money has gone on convergence arguments as far as places like Italy and Spain are concerned," said David Smith, economist at Williams de Broe. "If people thought the political will was going to collapse you would see a very abrupt reaction in the market."
